Geopolitics.title: South Korea leans toward military conscription for women

Geopolitics.title: U.S., South Korea and Japan to hold drill as North Korea ramps up pressure on U.S.
Geopolitics.summary: The announcement that the three countries will go ahead with a trilateral military drill comes a day after North Korea vowed to retaliate against what it called U.S. hostilities.

Geopolitics.summary: More than 100 companies have written an open letter calling for collective action to strengthen cyber defences amid a rise in AI-enabled cyber attacks.

Geopolitics.summary: As the death toll rises from flash floods that hit the Nepal-Tibet border, experts are warning more flooding could be on the way. And, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is expected to give a key address today.

Science.title: Nano-antennas make living cells light up brighter and faster
Science.summary: Researchers at Delft University of Technology have demonstrated for the first time that nano-antennas can enhance the fluorescence of proteins in living human and other mammalian cells. Scientists already use smart fluorescent proteins that light up when the electrical voltage across a nerve cell changes. By placing nano-antennas close to these light-emitting proteins, researchers can monitor processes inside cells with much greater precision. The discovery adds a new tool for revealing electrical signals in the brain through nanotechnology as well as genetic engineering. The research has been

Science.title: On Cloud 9: Have astronomers discovered the first starless galaxy?
Science.summary: Astronomers are closer than ever to confirming the discovery of the first starless or "failed" galaxy, packed with dark matter and gas but with virtually no stars.

Science.title: The discovery of the Great Barrier Reef's whale maternity ward
Science.summary: It started with a simple message: "This is the year to do something small for something huge." Now, 17 years later, the Whitsundays region has some of the best protection in the world for migrating humpback whales.

Science.title: Mercury's crust points to deeper, hotter volcanic origins than expected
Science.summary: The evolutionary histories of Earth and Mercury differ fundamentally. The smallest planet, closest to the sun, likely began cooling early on, much like a setting pudding: As early as about 1 billion years after its formation, Mercury's volcanic activity came to a halt, and a solid, continuous "rock skin" formed on the planet's surface. Earth's crust, on the other hand, is still in motion: Volcanism and plate tectonics are constantly stirring up the "Earth pudding." Exactly what Mercury's unique volcanic past looked like and how it shaped its current appearance remain unclear. However, research

Science.title: NASA Awards First Prize in Phase 2 of Agency’s LunaRecycle Challenge
Science.summary: NASA named a team from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) as the first prize winner for Phase 2 of the agency’s LunaRecycle Challenge, which focused on developing solutions for reducing waste during missions to the Moon or deep space by recycling common materials, like fabrics, plastics, foam, and metals.  The Composites for Extraterrestrial Recycling By Engineering the Reuse and Upcycling of Zotek (CERBERUZ) team, comprised of undergradu

Science.summary: To strengthen the nation’s space workforce and develop the next generation of space leaders, President Donald J. Trump signed an Executive Order on Friday to establish the nation’s first U.S. Space Academy. Science.title: Nepal's devastating floods reveal the danger of 'cascading hazards' in Himalayas
Science.summary: The devastating floods that have swept through the Nepal–Tibet border region are first and foremost a human tragedy. Hundreds of people have died or remain missing. But as scientists begin to reconstruct what happened, the event also exposes something fundamental about the way we understand natural hazards in high mountain regions. Mountains and rivers do not reset after an extreme event.

Science.title: Fastest star ever spotted at the centre of our galaxy
Science.summary: A newfound star called S301 is both the fastest ever seen and the closest to a supermassive black hole –and it could make bafflingly difficult tests of gravity possible at last

Science.title: Strange 'hobbit' species walked more like us than like 'Lucy,' hip bones reveal
Science.summary: Anthropologists studying the hip bones of Homo floresiensis have discovered that its pelvis was human-like, raising new questions about the origin of the enigmatic species.

Science.title: SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket launching NASA's Roman Space Telescope on Aug. 30: How to watch it live
Science.summary: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is scheduled to lift off atop a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket early Sunday morning (Aug. 30). Here's how to watch it live.

Science.title: Scientists find a huge hidden ice reservoir beneath Utah’s mountains
Science.summary: Beneath the rocky slopes of Mount Timpanogos lies far more ice than anyone walking across the surface might suspect. Researchers used gravity measurements to map the buried glacier in 3D and found it is about 83% ice, with enough frozen water to fill 600 Olympic swimming pools. Their findings suggest rock glaciers form as falling debris buries persistent snow and preserves it for thousands of years. Similar formations around the world may collectively store tens of gigatons of hidden water.

Science.title: Low temperature graphene growth opens a route to sustainable resource recycling
Science.summary: Graphene is an exceptionally useful material for creating batteries, catalysts and electronic devices. Yet producing graphene typically requires temperatures as high as 900°C (1,652°F), limiting energy efficiency and making structural control difficult. To make graphene production more practical, a recent study has overcome this long-standing temperature barrier.

Science.title: Self-blinking 'fairy lights' allow DNA to be imaged at almost double-helix-width resolution
Science.summary: Researchers have developed fluorescent molecules that permit imaging of how DNA is packaged inside living cells at unprecedented resolution and, in preserved cells, at a resolution close to the width of the double helix itself.

Science.title: Galápagos corals show El Niño events are more extreme now than in past 1,000 years
Science.summary: Temperatures have warmed dramatically across the equatorial Pacific Ocean in 2026, signaling the onset of a strong and potentially historic El Niño. These events can affect weather around the world, and the intensity of recent El Niño events is raising alarm that, as global temperatures rise, they are becoming stronger and more destructive.

Science.title: A Google-like search engine for single-cell RNA data could answer previously impossible questions
Science.summary: Imagine doctors could understand exactly which cells caused a patient's cancer or whether pathogens contributed to the disease. They could then use the information to tailor a treatment plan to the patient's specific cancer. But answering such questions would mean wading through data from thousands of experiments locked in massive databases around the globe. Moreover, the search would take at least several days.

Science.title: Relive private Chinese rocket's explosive 1st landing attempt (video)
Science.summary: LandSpace's first attempt to land its Zhuque-3 rocket was quite a spectacle, as newly released video footage reminds us.

Science.summary: The astronauts of NASA's Artemis II mission, who flew around the moon this past April, just received the United States' highest space honor.

Science.title: SpaceX recovers Starship from the Indian Ocean a month after launch and is shipping it back to Texas
Science.summary: SpaceX has pulled off its biggest salvage operation yet, recovering its most recently launched Starship from the Indian Ocean.

Science.title: NASA’s Roman telescope will see 100 times more sky than Hubble
Science.summary: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope will combine Hubble-like detail with a field of view 100 times larger, giving astronomers a sweeping new way to explore the cosmos. Its observations could uncover hidden planets, map billions of cosmic objects, and help scientists unravel the mysteries of dark matter and dark energy.

Science.title: Why scientists asked 1,000 people to bury their underwear
Science.summary: More than 1,000 volunteers buried cotton underwear across Switzerland to help scientists measure how active different soils are. The faster the fabric disappeared, the more biological activity was taking place underground. Gardens showed the fastest decomposition, while lawns had the least, revealing how strongly land management can shape soil life.

Science.title: The Forested Floodplains of Congaree National Park
Science.summary: The meandering Congaree River sustains towering forest ecosystems and fashions oxbow lakes as it shifts across its floodplain.

Science.title: Scientists invent a gel that creates neurons from other cells, which could help treat Alzheimer's
Science.summary: Scientists found a way to convert brain cells called astrocytes into neurons. In theory, this could replenish neurons lost in neurodegenerative conditions like Alzheimer's disease.

Science.title: The night we nearly saw a 'blood moon' (and why I love near-misses in astronomy)
Science.summary: Astronomy is often about being close to extraordinary things without fully experiencing them. Here's why to love partials, grazings, faint objects and other almost-events.

Science.summary: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which launches on 30 August, will observe space with the same detail as the Hubble Space Telescope, but over a much larger area

Science.title: Scientists capture first molecular-level images of water reorganization during a reaction crucial for life
Science.summary: Some of nature's most important chemical reactions rely on the coupled movement of negatively and positively charged particles. These processes play central roles in photosynthesis, catalysis and biological energy conversion yet remain difficult to observe.

Science.title: Indonesia escalates battle against fires, putrid haze
Science.summary: Indonesia has intensified efforts to fight wildfires with cloud seeding and water bombing as thousands of people nationwide battle to breathe through smoke and haze, officials said Friday.

Science.title: Once a legend, humpback whales make a comeback in Brazil
Science.summary: Female humpback whales off the coast of Brazil now have their pick of mates, who slap the water with their tails and jostle for attention—a scene that would have been unthinkable a few decades ago.

Science.title: Germany could miss climate goal in 2026 for the first time: Think tank
Science.summary: Germany risks missing an annual climate target in 2026 for the first time unless cuts to greenhouse gas emissions sharply accelerate, a think tank warned Friday.

Science.title: Experimental eye drops help blind mice see again
Science.summary: Scientists have created light-activated drugs that helped blind mice perceive light again and restored visually guided behavior without gene therapy, implants, or specialized lighting. Even more intriguingly, two of the most promising compounds worked when administered as eye drops, pointing toward a potentially simple new approach to restoring vision.

Science.title: Scientists tracked 4,500 animals and found a surprising human effect
Science.summary: Scientists tracking thousands of animals found that our physical presence can reshape where wildlife moves and lives, sometimes as strongly as roads, cities, and other human development. Because different species reacted in very different ways, conservation efforts may need to become much more targeted.

Science.title: The Moderna cancer vaccine offers hope — now we must speed up personalized therapies
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02680-5 A positive trial holds promise for treating people with cancer. More research is needed to get effective vaccines to the clinic.

Science.title: Ancient shark 'graveyard' uncovered in Egyptian desert
Science.summary: Fossilized teeth from at least seven shark species have been discovered in the Egyptian desert, hinting at its complex, watery past.

Science.title: How methylation sets a parasite in motion to invade host cells
Science.summary: Parasites such as Toxoplasma gondii and the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum depend on rapid, precisely controlled movement to complete their life cycles. To start moving, they must assemble actin filaments at their front end and connect them to the molecular machinery that generates force. How these events are coordinated has remained unclear.

Science.title: Earlier swathing opens a new pathway for subterranean clover seed harvest
Science.summary: Subterranean clover's ability to bury its seed supports pasture persistence but makes commercial seed harvesting difficult. The industry relies on aging Horwood-Bagshaw (HB) suction harvesters, which collect seed from fully dry crops after repeated tillage and raking.

Science.title: Diverse portfolio of protected areas key to Mexican conservation efforts
Science.summary: In 2020, Mexico joined 150 nations committing to protect 30% of its territory by 2030 as part of the global 30x30 initiative. More than halfway through the decade, there is ongoing debate about how to effectively expand protected areas to meet that ambitious goal.

Science.title: Astronaut Jonny Kim leaves NASA, will return to active military duty
Science.summary: NASA astronaut Jonny Kim is leaving the space agency to continue his military career. Kim, who's also a medical doctor, completed one spaceflight during his NASA career.

Science.summary: The total solar eclipse on 2 August 2027 is due to be the longest one until the year 2114, and researchers, eclipse chasers and tourists alike are on the edge of their seats

Science.title: Climate policy could learn from people who already live within the limits of sufficiency
Science.summary: Tina Nyfors, who recently defended her doctoral thesis at the University of Helsinki, studied sufficiency, a way of living and a principle for organizing society to stay within environmental limits while ensuring that people have enough. Nyfors directs attention to people whose carbon footprint is already in line with sufficiency and refers to them as the sufficiency class. Their way of life has a moderate climate impact yet still meets their needs.

Science.title: Breathable smart sensor developed for real-time hazardous gas detection on masks
Science.summary: A research team led by Sungwon Lee, a professor in the Department of Physics and Chemistry at DGIST, developed a hierarchical nano-on-nano structure by directly growing graphene nanowalls (GNWs) on polymer nanofibers and successfully used the structure to enhance the sensing performance of wearable gas sensors. The technology is expected to be applied to next-generation wearable sensors for real-time monitoring of individuals' breathing environments or hazardous gases in industrial settings.

Science.title: Joro spiders eat wider range of insects than Georgia's native orb weavers
Science.summary: When Joro spiders first arrived stateside more than a decade ago, scientists worried the massive black-and-yellow spiders would gorge themselves on the same bugs as native spiders (or even the native spiders themselves). If the invasive arachnids did make massive meals of Georgia's insects, the local orb weaver population—already facing dangers from insecticide and pesticide use—could suffer.

Science.title: The Meta settlement is a start, but it's not enough to create real change — that's what we need to focus on now
Science.summary: The Meta settlement requires limited oversight of Instagram and Facebook for just five years. Making it permanent and industry-wide requires a law, says experts Mariana Olaizola Rosenblat and Jonathan Bellack .

Science.title: Why some earthquakes caused by fracking come with warning signs
Science.summary: Fracking, the injection of high-pressure fluid to fracture rock and release oil or gas, can trigger earthquakes. While some sites generate small tremors beforehand that may provide an early warning, others produce few or none.

Science.title: Briefing Chat: How Dolly Parton left her mark on science
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02732-w Nature reporters discuss the country-music icon's advocacy for vaccines and public health — plus, promising trial results for an mRNA cancer therapy.

Science.title: Heisuke Hironaka obituary: mathematician who smoothed out geometry’s complexities
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02688-x His awe-inspiring proof for the resolution of singularities — such as peaks, edges and self-crossings — revolutionized algebraic geometry.

Science.title: Dog-friendly dining isn't just a trend, it's good for business, new research shows
Science.summary: Restaurants that go beyond simply allowing dogs on patios by offering dedicated menu items for them can significantly boost customer traffic, spending and word-of-mouth, according to new research from Toronto Metropolitan University.

Science.title: Chimpanzees have been hurling rocks at the same trees for more than a decade
Science.summary: Some chimpanzees in West Africa repeatedly throw rocks at particular trees, creating piles of stones that can remain in use for more than a decade. Researchers think this unusual behavior may be cultural and could serve as a form of communication, territorial signaling, or something more symbolic. Camera traps and audio recordings are now being used to reveal who throws the stones and how nearby chimpanzees respond.

Science.title: Fast fashion's carbon footprint can be reduced across its life cycle, new study suggests
Science.summary: Fast fashion is built on cheap, short-lived garments, especially cotton and polyester T-shirts. To sustain its profits, the industry relies on high production frequency, short product lifespan and a globalized supply chain. All these elements contribute to making the industry a major source of global pollution.

Science.title: Honey bees can serve as sentinels for environmental health
Science.summary: Honey bees (Apis mellifera) are widely known as essential pollinators, but researchers using a "One Health" approach have also identified them as biological sentinels of environmental health. Honey bees continuously interact with their surrounding environment through the collection of nectar, pollen and water and can therefore be exposed to contaminants present in agricultural and natural ecosystems. Their health may consequently provide valuable information about environmental pressures affecting biodiversity and ecosystem functioning.

Science.title: NASA Invites Media to Turkey Artemis Accords Signing Ceremony
Science.summary: Turkey will sign the Artemis Accords during a ceremony at 2:30 p.m. EDT Monday, Aug. 31, at NASA Headquarters in Washington, becoming the 71st country signatory. Science.title: Motorboat noise stunts growth and impairs predator escape in reef fish, study shows
Science.summary: Coral reef fish that are exposed to motorboat noise grow up smaller and less able to dodge predators, new research shows. Scientists played either boat noise or natural reef sounds to a species from the Great Barrier Reef called the spiny chromis, both as embryos and soon after hatching.

Science.title: Nepal's catastrophic flood shows disaster preparedness must be a shared responsibility
Science.summary: The catastrophic flood in Nepal and Tibet is a devastating reminder that disasters rarely occur in isolation.

Science.title: The popular diabetes drug metformin has been used for decades — and scientists just figured out its main mechanism
Science.summary: Scientists have debated whether the diabetes drug metformin acts primarily in the intestines or the liver. New findings clear up this confusion.

Science.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based meat alternatives. Every one contained fungal toxins
Science.summary: Every one of 212 plant-based meat alternatives and drinks tested in the UK contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, though concentrations remained below recommended EU guideline levels. Researchers say the bigger question is whether regularly eating large amounts of these foods could lead to potentially concerning cumulative exposure over time.

Science.title: Will Meta’s deal make social media safe for kids? Researchers are dubious
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 28 August 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02733-9 Nature talks to specialists about the changes coming to Facebook and Instagram, and whether there’s evidence they will help.

Science.title: Less buying power, elevated inflation push down consumer views
Science.summary: Consumer sentiment dropped about 6% from last month, landing around 11% below a year ago amid continued worries that inflation will remain elevated for the foreseeable future, according to the University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers.

Science.title: Widespread use of AI tools could make it harder to craft effective business communications
Science.summary: Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT make it easier for business owners to produce polished pitches, business plans and other communications, but according to new research from The University of Manchester and Canada's University of Alberta, their widespread use could ultimately make it harder for businesses to effectively communicate with their audiences.
